summary: An early Telnet option, from 1974, for negotiating how linefeed characters in output are handled. Different systems treated line endings differently, so the option lets both ends settle on a convention. It is historic.

plainLanguage.summary: Computers once disagreed about what ends a line of text. This note lets two computers talk it over and pick one way.

questions: how did telnet handle line endings
what is the telnet naolfd option
who handles output linefeeds in telnet
subtitle: A Telnet option from 1974 for deciding who handles linefeeds in output, and how.

tldr.problem: Different systems and printers treated linefeeds in output differently, so the two ends of a Telnet connection needed a way to agree on who deals with them.
tldr.mechanism: The NAOLFD option (code 16) uses the usual DO, DON'T, WILL and WON'T commands to agree to negotiate, then subnegotiation carries an 8-bit value saying who handles linefeeds and how.
tldr.outcome: The unit metadata lists RFC 658 as Historic.

today: The unit metadata lists RFC 658 as Historic, and no RFC is recorded as obsoleting it, so it describes an option that should not be treated as current.

sections.title: The NAOLFD Option
sections.content:
RFC 658 defines the Telnet option NAOLFD, Negotiate About Output Linefeed Disposition, with option code 16. It is discussed for a simplex connection, as described in the NAOL and NAOP Telnet options, with a data sender and a data receiver.

The default is DON'T NAOLFD / WON'T NAOLFD. With no negotiation neither party is required nor prohibited from handling linefeeds, but it is appropriate if at least the data receiver handles them, albeit primitively.
sections.plainLanguage: It is a way for a sender and a receiver of text to ask each other, "Who is going to deal with the line-ending characters?"

sections.title: The Commands
sections.content:
IAC DO NAOLFD means the sender requests or agrees to negotiate; after agreement and with no further subnegotiation, the receiver is assumed to handle linefeeds. IAC DON'T NAOLFD refuses, or demands a return to the unnegotiated default.

IAC WILL NAOLFD is the receiver's request or agreement to negotiate, after which the receiver alone is assumed to handle linefeeds. IAC WON'T NAOLFD is its refusal.

Subnegotiation is IAC SB NAOLFD DS <8-bit value> IAC SE from the sender (DS is code 1) and IAC SB NAOLFD DR <8-bit value> IAC SE from the receiver (DR is code 0). The value says which party should handle output linefeeds and what their disposition should be.
sections.plainLanguage: The two sides say "yes, let's talk" or "no thanks", and then one passes a number that spells out the plan.

sections.title: The 8-Bit Value and the Rules
sections.content:
A value of 0 means the command sender will handle linefeeds alone. Values 1 to 250 ask the other party to handle them, with a delay of that many character-times, or NULs inserted before the next data character. 252 suggests linefeeds be discarded, 253 that they be simulated, 254 that the sender wait for a character on the other simplex connection, and 255 suggests nothing about how. 251 is not allowed, for compatibility with related Telnet options.

Two rules guide the outcome. If neither side wants to handle output linefeeds, the data receiver must. If both want to, the data sender does, since it is presumed to know the data. Simulation means replacing the linefeed with new-line and enough blanks to restore the lateral position, and is allowed only for linefeeds not immediately preceded by a carriage return. Delays must be NUL characters inserted immediately after the character.
sections.plainLanguage: The number is a note like "I will do it", "you do it but wait a bit", or "just skip those". If nobody volunteers the receiver does it, and if both volunteer the sender wins.

items.label: Sender handles
items.desc: Command sender suggests that it alone will handle linefeeds.

items.label: Not allowed
